title: Deep SiMLR: Auditable Multi-Modal Integration for Biomedical Discovery
text:
Abstract
Integrating structural neuroimaging, cognitive assessments, and multi-omic profiles requires latent representations that remain both clinically predictive and anatomically or molecularly localizable. Classical linear factorizations such as principal component analysis and canonical correlation analysis disperse biological variance across dense, sign-mixed combinations of features, whereas end-to-end deep neural networks obscure how individual brain regions or genes drive patient-level predictions. We introduce the Similarity-driven Multi-view Representation (SiMR) framework, which couples a sparse, non-negative, approximately orthogonal linear input projection (nsa_flow) with interchangeable linear (SiMLR), non-linear decoder (LEND), and invertible normalizing-flow (Flow-SiMR-V) alignment modules. Across \(1,084\) participants with Mild Cognitive Impairment from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI-MCI) and eleven additional multi-omic, clinical, and synthetic benchmarks, aligning baseline cortical thickness and subcortical volumes with eleven neuropsychological scales during training improves out-of-sample cognitive prediction from structural magnetic resonance imaging alone from \(R^2 = 0.152\) to \(R^2 = 0.252\) while isolating focal temporoparietal, medial temporal, and frontocingulate networks that recapitulate Braak neurofibrillary staging and spare primary sensorimotor cortex. Crucially, evaluating learned representations across both multi-variable linear probes and single-axis decision trees demonstrates that while linear regression is algebraically invariant to post-hoc column mixing, coordinate-aligned SiMR projections preserve more than fourfold higher single-factor predictive utility (\(R^2 = 0.197\) versus \(0.044\)) and recover up to \(84.7\%\) of ground-truth biological pathways under moderate (\(50\%\)) feature sparsity.

title: 1  Introduction and Background
text:
1.1 Clinical and Scientific Motivation: Why Multi-View Integration Must Be Auditable
Modern biomedical cohorts characterize disease across distinct physical, physiological, and behavioral scales. In neurodegenerative disorders such as Alzheimer’s disease, structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) quantifies millimeter-scale regional cortical thinning and subcortical volume loss (Jack et al. 2018; Dickerson et al. 2009; Fischl and Dale 2000; Tustison et al. 2014, 2021; Avants et al. 2011; Das et al. 2009), whereas clinical diagnosis and trial monitoring rely on multi-domain neuropsychological batteries measuring episodic memory, executive function, language, and daily functional independence (Rosen et al. 1984; Folstein et al. 1975; Morris 1993; Pfeffer et al. 1982; Reitan 1958; Rey 1964). In clinical oncology, projects such as The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) profile primary tumors simultaneously across messenger RNA (mRNA) transcriptomics, somatic DNA copy-number variation (CNV), reverse-phase protein arrays (RPPA), and DNA methylation (Weinstein et al. 2013; The Cancer Genome Atlas Network 2012; The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network 2013; Hoadley et al. 2018). Across both settings, clinicians and translational scientists require analytical methods that connect structural or molecular vulnerability to clinical phenotype without sacrificing anatomical or biological localization (Avants et al. 2010, 2014, 2021; Seeley et al. 2009; Rudin 2019).
A recurring tension in multi-modal data integration separates predictive accuracy from mechanistic interpretability. For a neurologist evaluating a patient with Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), predicting an aggregate cognitive decline score from a black-box neural network is insufficient for clinical decision-making or clinical trial stratification (Rudin 2019; Doshi-Velez and Kim 2017; Lipton 2018). The clinician must verify whether the predictive signal arises from established disease-vulnerable substrates—such as the entorhinal-hippocampal memory circuit of early Braak stages I–III (Braak and Braak 1991; Jack et al. 2018; Racine et al. 2018) or the temporoparietal and posterior cingulate association hubs of Braak stages IV–V (Dickerson et al. 2009; Buckner et al. 2005; Seeley et al. 2009; Cuingnet et al. 2011)—rather than from scanner artifacts, ventricular enlargement, or global brain atrophy. Similarly, a molecular tumor board cannot design a targeted assay from a dense principal component combining \(20,000\) transcripts; actionable translation requires isolating compact, non-redundant driver pathways such as estrogen-receptor transcriptional networks (ESR1, GATA3, PGR) or focal chromosomal amplifications (17q23, 8p11-p12) (Perou et al. 2000; Parker et al. 2009; The Cancer Genome Atlas Network 2012; Curtis et al. 2012; Prat and Parker 2020; Cohen et al. 2014).
Existing multi-view factorizations force an uncomfortable compromise between these clinical and computational goals:

Dense Linear Factorizations Disperse Anatomical Signal: Principal Component Analysis (PCA) (Hotelling 1933), Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) (Hotelling 1936; Hardoon et al. 2004; Chaudhuri et al. 2009), Partial Least Squares (PLS) (Krishnan et al. 2011; Tenenhaus and Tenenhaus 2011; Tenenhaus et al. 2014), Joint and Individual Variation Explained (JIVE) (Lock et al. 2013), and Multi-Omics Factor Analysis (MOFA) (Argelaguet et al. 2020; Cantini et al. 2021; Abdi et al. 2013) estimate dense loading matrices in which every brain region or gene receives a non-zero weight of mixed positive and negative sign. In neuroimaging, the dominant principal component captures global brain size and diffuse cross-cortical covariance, obscuring focal disease networks behind sign cancellations (Zou et al. 2006; Witten et al. 2009; Kandel et al. 2015).
Rigid Orthogonality vs. Rank Collapse in Sparse Matrix Decompositions: Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) (Lee and Seung 1999, 2001; Hoyer 2004; Ding et al. 2006; Cichocki et al. 2009) and Sparse PCA / Sparse CCA (Zou et al. 2006; Witten et al. 2009; Parkhomenko et al. 2009) promote parts-based or localized weights. However, without explicit cross-column orthogonality control, sparse non-negative projections frequently suffer from rank collapse—where multiple latent components converge onto the same high-variance hub—whereas enforcing strict Stiefel manifold orthogonality (\(\mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m = \mathbf{I}_k\)) (Edelman et al. 1998; Absil et al. 2008; Wen and Yin 2013; Boumal 2023) forbids overlapping biological pathways from sharing pleiotropic hub genes or transmodal cortical hubs (Buckner et al. 2009; Menon and Uddin 2010; Avants et al. 2021, 2025).
Opaque Deep Multi-Modal Encoders: Deep Canonical Correlation Analysis (DCCA) (Andrew et al. 2013; Wang et al. 2015), multi-modal Variational Autoencoders (Wu and Goodman 2018; Shi et al. 2019; Higgins et al. 2017; Hinton and Salakhutdinov 2006; Vincent et al. 2008; Bengio et al. 2013), and contrastive multi-view transformers (Radford et al. 2021; Baltrušaitis et al. 2019) route raw measurements through multilayer non-linear encoders before aligning modalities. This composition destroys the direct linear mapping between input features and latent axes, forcing investigators to rely on post-hoc attribution approximations (SHAP, LIME, Integrated Gradients) (Lundberg and Lee 2017; Ribeiro et al. 2016; Sundararajan et al. 2017; Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola 2018) that can be unstable across correlated anatomical or genomic features (Rudin 2019; Hooker et al. 2019).







Figure 1.1: Visual overview of interpretable multi-view representation learning with PySiMLR. (1) Multi-Modal Clinical Views: Heterogeneous biomedical cohorts—such as cortical thickness MRI paired with neuropsychological batteries in Alzheimer’s disease (ADNI-MCI), or mRNA, copy-number variation, and proteomics in oncology (TCGA-BRCA)—are observed across shared subjects. (2) Sparse Orthogonal Entrypoint (\(\mathbf{V}_m \ge 0\), nsa_flow): Every modality enters exclusively through an auditable linear projection \(\mathbf{Z}_m = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\) regularized by Non-Negative Stiefel Approximating Flow (nsa_flow), yielding localized, parts-based feature dictionaries with controlled column overlap (\(D(\mathbf{V}_m) \to 0\)). (3) Shared SiMR Patient Manifold: Modality projections align onto a shared patient embedding (\(\mathbf{U}\)) via linear consensus (SiMLR), non-linear decoding (LEND), or invertible normalizing flows (Flow-SiMR-V). (4) Direct Anatomical & Biomarker Attribution: Because the input boundary remains strictly linear and non-negative, latent axes map directly back to anatomical circuits (e.g., Braak stages) and patient-level feature contributions (\(c_{ij} = x_{ij} v_{jl}\)) without post-hoc black-box approximations.

1.2 The SiMR Framework: A Linear Entrypoint Paired with Flexible Multi-View Alignment
To satisfy both statistical learning requirements and clinical auditability, we formulate the Similarity-driven Multi-view Representation (SiMR) framework around a strict architectural boundary: the Linear Entrypoint Principle (Figure 1.1). Regardless of how complex the downstream cross-modal alignment or generative modeling becomes, every modality \(m \in \{1, \dots, M\}\) enters the model exclusively through an explicit, non-negative, sparse, and approximately orthogonal linear projection matrix \(\mathbf{V}_m \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{p_m \times k}\):
\[
\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m
\tag{1.1}\]
This architectural separation provides three foundational properties that appeal simultaneously to machine learning researchers and clinical domain specialists:

Exact Feature-to-Factor and Patient-Level Attribution: Because each latent coordinate \(l \in \{1, \dots, k\}\) is an additive linear combination of non-negative weights (\(\mathbf{V}_m \ge 0\)), every column \(\mathbf{v}_{m,l}\) represents an immediately inspectable anatomical map or molecular module without sign-cancellation ambiguity (Lee and Seung 1999; Avants et al. 2021). At the individual patient level \(i\), the exact contribution of feature \(j\) to component \(l\) is the simple elementwise product \(c_{m,i,j,l} = x_{m,i,j} v_{m,j,l}\).
Continuous Balance Between Pathway Overlap and Factor Redundancy (nsa_flow): Rather than choosing between unconstrained sparsity (which permits duplicate components) and exact Stiefel manifold projection (which prohibits shared biological hubs), we constrain \(\mathbf{V}_m\) via Non-Negative Stiefel Approximating Flow (nsa_flow) (Edelman et al. 1998; Absil et al. 2008; Avants et al. 2021, 2025). A single trade-off weight \(w \in (0,1)\) continuously balances cross-modal alignment fidelity against scale-invariant column decorrelation and norm balance, while post-optimization quantile thresholding (\(q \in [0, 1)\)) allows investigators to dial continuously between pathway-wide discovery (\(q = 0.5\)) and ultra-compact diagnostic panels (\(q = 0.8\)).
Interchangeable Downstream Alignment Topologies: Holding the linear entrypoint \(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\) fixed, SiMR supports three modular alignment paradigms: (i) classical linear consensus optimization (SiMLR) (Avants et al. 2021), (ii) non-linear multilayer perceptron decoding (LEND, alongside shared-private variants NED and NEDPP (Bousmalis et al. 2016; Salzmann et al. 2010)) that accommodates curved manifold structure in the decoders while keeping the encoder strictly linear, and (iii) invertible RealNVP normalizing flows (Flow-SiMR-V) (Dinh et al. 2017; Rezende and Mohamed 2015; Papamakarios et al. 2021) that align non-Gaussian biological distributions in an exact bijective latent space.

text:
1.3 Subspace Preservation vs. Coordinate Axis Disentanglement
A central contribution of this work is resolving a widespread methodological confusion in representation learning benchmarks: why post-hoc rotation or mixing of latent variables often leaves multi-variable linear regression unchanged while destroying clinical interpretability and single-factor utility.
Suppose an algorithm learns a sparse, neuroanatomically localized projection \(\mathbf{V}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{p_m \times k}\), and a post-processing step multiplies \(\mathbf{V}_m\) on the right by any invertible \(k \times k\) mixing matrix \(\mathbf{M} \in \mathrm{GL}(k)\) (for example, an orthogonal Procrustes rotation (Schönemann 1966; Davis and Kahan 1970) or independent component unmixing matrix (Hyvärinen and Oja 2000)). For any downstream model that depends only on the column space of the projected features—such as ordinary least squares or lightly penalized ridge regression (Hoerl and Kennard 1970; Hastie et al. 2009)—the column space is mathematically invariant to \(\mathbf{M}\):
\[
\operatorname{span}(\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m \mathbf{M}) = \operatorname{span}(\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m) \quad \forall \, \mathbf{M} \in \mathrm{GL}(k)
\tag{1.2}\]
Consequently, evaluating learned representations solely with multi-variable linear probes measures only overall subspace capacity, masking whether individual columns \(\mathbf{v}_{m,l}\) correspond to coherent biological systems or arbitrary diagonal mixtures. In contrast, coordinate-wise evaluations—such as axis-aligned decision trees (RandomForest (Breiman 2001)), single-biomarker clinical thresholds, and anatomical loading maps—depend directly on the orientation and sparsity of the individual coordinate axes. To separate these properties rigorously, our benchmark evaluates all nine candidate architectures across four complementary probes (Table 1.1).

section: 1.4 Summary of Contributions
text:
1.4 Summary of Contributions

Unified SiMR Architecture and Open-Source Implementation: We present a self-contained mathematical and software formulation (pysimlr + nsa_flow) uniting linear similarity-driven representation learning (SiMLR), non-linear decoding with a linear entrypoint (LEND), and detached-prior normalizing-flow alignment (Flow-SiMR-V).
Clinical Neuroimaging Translation in ADNI-MCI (\(N = 1,084\)): Under a strict clinical deployment protocol where multimodal alignment is learned from structural MRI and cognitive scales during training but evaluated using structural MRI alone at test time, SiMLR improves out-of-sample composite cognitive prediction by \(+65.8\%\) over raw anatomical ridge regression (\(R^2 = 0.252\) vs. \(0.152\)) and isolates three distinct neuroanatomical circuits matching Braak neurofibrillary staging (Braak and Braak 1991; Dickerson et al. 2009) while assigning zero weight to spared primary sensorimotor cortex.
Actionable Operating-Point Characterization Across 12 Benchmarks: Through a 9-method comparison across six real biomedical cohorts and six synthetic ground-truth regimes (\(1,215\) operating-point cross-validation folds plus a \(1,214\)-configuration hyperparameter sweep), we establish two practical operating regimes for nsa_flow quantile thresholding: moderate sparsity (\(q = 0.5\)) for maximum pathway recovery (\(F_1 = 0.847\)) and predictive accuracy, and aggressive sparsity (\(q = 0.8\)–\(0.85\)) for ultra-compact biomarker panels retaining over \(99\%\) of peak linear predictive performance.

text:
2.2 Unified Multi-View Objective and the Nine Benchmark Architectures
Let \(\{\mathbf{X}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times p_m}\}_{m=1}^M\) denote \(M\) data modalities acquired on the same \(N\) subjects during training. Every architecture within the SiMR family maps each view \(m\) into a \(k\)-dimensional latent space exclusively through the linear entrypoint \(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\) while optimizing a composite objective combining cross-modal alignment \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}\), within-view geometric or reconstruction preservation \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{within}}\), and manifold regularization \(\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{V}_m)\):
\[
\min_{\{\mathbf{V}_m\}_{m=1}^M, \, \Theta} \; \sum_{m=1}^M \mathcal{L}_{\text{within}}(\mathbf{X}_m, \mathbf{V}_m; \Theta) + \lambda_{\text{align}} \, \mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}\!\left(\{\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\}_{m=1}^M; \Theta\right) + \sum_{m=1}^M \mathcal{R}(\mathbf{V}_m)
\tag{2.1}\]
Here \(\Theta\) denotes architecture-specific alignment parameters: the shared orthonormal subject basis \(\mathbf{U} \in \operatorname{St}(N, k)\) in SiMLR (Avants et al. 2021), the non-linear decoder weights \(\{\phi_m\}\) in LEND, or the invertible coupling network parameters \(\{\psi_m\}\) in Flow-SiMR-V (Dinh et al. 2017). section: 2.3 Non-Negative Stiefel Approximating Flow (nsa_flow) and Operating Points
text:
2.3 Non-Negative Stiefel Approximating Flow (nsa_flow) and Operating Points
In high-dimensional neuroimaging (\(p_m \sim 10^2\)–\(10^5\)) and transcriptomics (\(p_m \sim 10^4\)), updating \(\mathbf{V}_m\) along a cross-modal covariance gradient \(\mathbf{V}_{m,0} \in \mathbb{R}^{p_m \times k}\) quickly causes multiple latent components to collapse onto the dominant variance axis. Conversely, projecting \(\mathbf{V}_m\) onto the strict Stiefel manifold \(\operatorname{St}(p_m, k)\) (Edelman et al. 1998) forces exact zero inner products between columns, preventing distinct biological networks from sharing pleiotropic hub genes or transmodal association cortices (Buckner et al. 2009; Avants et al. 2021, 2025).
To provide a continuous, scale-invariant bridge between these extremes, each update of \(\mathbf{V}_m\) minimizes the dimensionless Non-Negative Stiefel Approximating Flow (nsa_flow) energy \(E_w(\mathbf{V}_m; \mathbf{V}_{m,0})\) over the non-negative orthant \(\mathbf{V}_m \ge 0\) (Avants et al. 2025; Birgin et al. 2000; Barzilai and Borwein 1988; Armijo 1966; Parikh and Boyd 2014; Bolte et al. 2014; Ablin and Peyré 2022) (Figure 2.1):
\[
E_w(\mathbf{V}_m; \mathbf{V}_{m,0}) = (1 - w) \, \mathcal{L}_{\text{fid}}(\mathbf{V}_m; \mathbf{V}_{m,0}) + w \, D(\mathbf{V}_m), \quad w \in (0, 1)
\tag{2.2}\]
where the scale-normalized fidelity loss \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{fid}}\) and the trace-normalized Gram defect \(D(\mathbf{V}_m)\) are both dimensionless and \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) by construction:
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{fid}}(\mathbf{V}_m; \mathbf{V}_{m,0}) = \frac{\|\mathbf{V}_m - \mathbf{V}_{m,0}\|_F^2}{2 \|\mathbf{V}_{m,0}\|_F^2}, \qquad D(\mathbf{V}_m) = \left\| \mathbf{G}(\mathbf{V}_m) - \frac{1}{k}\mathbf{I}_k \right\|_F^2, \qquad \mathbf{G}(\mathbf{V}_m) = \frac{\mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m}{\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{V}_m)}
\tag{2.3}\]
The Gram defect \(D(\mathbf{V}_m)\) decomposes orthogonally into off-diagonal column correlation plus diagonal column norm imbalance:
\[
D(\mathbf{V}_m) = \sum_{l \neq r} G_{lr}^2 + \sum_{l=1}^k \left(G_{ll} - \frac{1}{k}\right)^2
\tag{2.4}\]
Minimizing \(D(\mathbf{V}_m)\) therefore prevents both duplicate factors (\(G_{lr} \to 0\) for \(l \neq r\)) and dead components (\(G_{ll} \to 1/k\)), while the Euclidean gradient \(\nabla_{\mathbf{V}_m} D(\mathbf{V}_m)\) is identically orthogonal to \(\mathbf{V}_m\) (\(\langle \nabla_{\mathbf{V}_m} D(\mathbf{V}_m), \mathbf{V}_m \rangle_F = 0\)), ensuring that orthogonality regularization never artificially inflates or shrinks matrix scale. Following gradient polish, column-wise quantile thresholding at level \(q \in [0, 1)\) zeros out entries below the \(q\)-th percentile of each column’s positive weights and normalizes columns to unit \(\ell_2\) norm. This yields two primary clinical operating points:

Discovery Operating Point (\(q = 0.5\)): Retains the top \(50\%\) of active weights per component, capturing complete multi-gene pathways or distributed functional-anatomical brain systems.
Focal Biomarker Panel Operating Point (\(q = 0.8\)–\(0.85\)): Retains only the top \(15\%\)–\(20\%\) of weights per component, isolating compact regional MRI signatures or minimal gene panels suitable for targeted clinical assays.

text:
2.4 Linear, Non-Linear Decoder, and Normalizing-Flow Alignment Topologies
Holding the linear entrypoint \(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\) fixed, SiMR provides three alignment topologies tailored to different cross-modal relationships:

Linear Consensus Alignment (SiMLR): Alternates between updating \(\mathbf{V}_m\) via cross-modal covariance projection \(\mathbf{V}_{m,0} = \mathbf{X}_m^\top \mathbf{S}_m \mathbf{U}\) followed by nsa_flow polish (L-BFGS-B (Byrd et al. 1995; Nocedal and Wright 2006) or Lookahead (Zhang et al. 2019)), and updating the shared subject basis \(\mathbf{U} = \operatorname{polar}\!\left(\sum_{m=1}^M \tilde{\mathbf{Z}}_m\right)\) via exact Sylvester-differentiable polar decomposition (Higham 2008; Avants et al. 2021).
Linear Entrypoint with Non-Linear Decoders (LEND): Replaces the linear reconstruction model with modality-specific multilayer perceptron decoders \(g_{\phi_m} : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^{p_m}\) trained to reconstruct \(\mathbf{X}_m\) from \(\mathbf{U}\) while penalizing encoder-consensus divergence \(\gamma \|\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m - \mathbf{U}\|_F^2\). Because non-linearity is restricted to the generative decoders \(g_{\phi_m}\), out-of-sample inference \(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{X}_{m,\text{test}} \mathbf{V}_m\) remains strictly linear and auditable.
Detached-Prior Normalizing Flows (Flow-SiMR-V): Routes each linear projection \(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\) through a volume-preserving RealNVP flow \(f_{\psi_m} : \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^k\) (Dinh et al. 2017; Papamakarios et al. 2021) toward an isotropic Gaussian prior. To prevent the single-modality density term from pulling \(\mathbf{V}_m\) toward high-variance noise directions, gradients from the Gaussian prior are detached before reaching \(\mathbf{V}_m\) (proved in Appendix C), ensuring that \(\mathbf{V}_m\) updates exclusively along cross-modal flow agreement:

\[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{Flow-SiMR-V}} = \sum_{m=1}^M \frac{1}{2N} \left\| f_{\psi_m}\!\left(\operatorname{sg}(\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m)\right) \right\|_F^2 + \lambda_{\text{align}} \sum_{m < m'} \frac{1}{N} \left\| f_{\psi_m}(\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m) - f_{\psi_{m'}}(\mathbf{X}_{m'} \mathbf{V}_{m'}) \right\|_F^2
\tag{2.5}\]

section: 2.5 Clinical Deployment Protocols: Multi-Modal Fusion vs. Single-View Bipartite Translation
text:
2.5 Clinical Deployment Protocols: Multi-Modal Fusion vs. Single-View Bipartite Translation
A critical distinction in clinical translation is which data views are available when evaluating a new patient (Stone 1974):

Protocol A (Multi-Modal Biomarker Discovery): All \(M\) predictor modalities (for example, mRNA, CNV, and proteomics in TCGA) are measured on both training and test patients, and models predict an external clinical outcome \(\mathbf{y}\) (such as survival or histological subtype) from either modality-specific projections \(\mathbf{X}_{m,\text{test}}\mathbf{V}_m\) or the fused consensus embedding \(\mathbf{U}_{\text{test}}\).
Protocol B (Single-View Clinical Translation in ADNI-MCI): During training, the algorithm aligns structural MRI (\(\mathbf{X}_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 62}\), DKT cortical thickness and subcortical volumes (Desikan et al. 2006; Klein and Tourville 2012; Tustison et al. 2014, 2010; Avants et al. 2011, 2014)) with an 11-scale neuropsychological battery (\(\mathbf{X}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 11}\)). At test time, cognitive test scores \(\mathbf{X}_{2,\text{test}}\) are completely withheld; predictions of composite cognitive status (CogPC1) and individual clinical scales are generated solely from the patient’s baseline structural MRI scan via \(\mathbf{Z}_{1,\text{test}} = \mathbf{X}_{1,\text{test}} \mathbf{V}_1\). This protocol tests whether supervising anatomical representation learning with multidimensional cognitive batteries during training extracts a more clinically informative neuroanatomical basis than unsupervised MRI decomposition.

3.1 Study Design, Biomedical Cohorts, and Synthetic Ground-Truth Regimes
We evaluate the nine architectures defined in Chapter 2 across twelve multi-view benchmarks: six real biomedical and clinical cohorts (ADNI-MCI, MultiOmics [TCGA-BRCA], TCGA-KIRC, Heart, Diabetes, and mfeat) and six synthetic generative regimes with known ground-truth latent coordinates \(\mathbf{U}^*\) and feature supports \(\mathbf{V}_m^*\) (Table 3.1). Every model is evaluated across three independent 70/30 stratified or random train/test splits (seeds \(42, 43, 44\)) across three nsa_flow quantile sparsity levels (\(q \in \{\text{None}, 0.5, 0.8\}\), totaling \(1,215\) cross-validation fits), supplemented by a \(1,214\)-configuration hyperparameter sweep on ADNI-MCI (\(N = 1,084\)). To prevent data leakage, all feature standardization (StandardScaler), column completeness filtering (\(\ge 98\%\)), and demographic covariate adjustments (Frisch–Waugh–Lovell residualization (Frisch and Waugh 1933; Lovell 1963) of age, biological sex, and education inside ADNI-MCI) are fitted strictly within each training split and applied out-of-sample to the held-out test split.

Three empirical principles emerge from Table 3.2 and Figures 3.1–3.3:

Multi-View Alignment Outperforms Single-Matrix Factorization When Views Differ in Scale or Private Variance: LEND (mean Friedman rank \(3.25\)), NEDPP (\(4.00\)), Flow-SiMR-V (\(4.08\)), and SiMLR-LBFGS (\(4.17\)) lead the linear entrypoint ranking ahead of concatenated PCA (\(6.42\)) and NSAFlow-PCA (\(6.00\)). On heterogeneous cohorts such as mfeat (\(p = [76, 64, 6, 47]\)) and Shared+Private (\(p = [160, 60, 30]\)), concatenated PCA rotates toward the highest-dimensional view (mfeat linear accuracy \(0.727\), Shared+Private \(R^2 = 0.618\)), whereas cross-view alignment equalizes view contributions (mfeat accuracy \(0.967\) for NEDPP and \(0.943\) for SiMLR-LBFGSB; Shared+Private \(R^2 = 0.956\) for LEND).
Coordinate-Aligned nsa_flow Projections Prevent the Random Forest Axis Drop: As established in Equation 1.2, ridge regression on \(\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\) is insensitive to orthogonal or oblique column mixing \(\mathbf{V}_m \mathbf{M}\), hiding the fact that dense PCA mixes distinct biological mechanisms across columns. When evaluated with coordinate-splitting decision trees (RandomForest), PCA suffers an average score drop of \(\Delta = -0.044\) across the 12 cohorts—collapsing completely on weak sparse factors (NonnegPartsWeak linear \(R^2 = 0.125 \to\) Random Forest \(R^2 = 0.000\)) and dropping by \(71\%\) on ADNI-MCI (\(0.152 \to 0.044\)). In contrast, Flow-SiMR-V (\(\Delta = -0.024\)) and SiMLR-LBFGSB (\(\Delta = -0.022\)) cut the axis-mixing penalty in half.
Operating Points Match Intrinsic Biological Density (\(q = 0.5\) vs. \(q = 0.8\)): Figure 3.4 demonstrates how the quantile threshold \(q\) acts as a tunable lens on feature support recovery. Across the \(1,215\)-fit operating-point evaluation, moderate sparsity (\(q = 0.5\)) achieves the highest overall linear predictive score (\(0.679\)) and highest Random Forest axis score (\(0.651\)) while recovering \(F_1 = 0.847\) (SiMLR-LBFGSB) on \(50\%\)-sparse ground-truth pathways (Linear). When the underlying biology is concentrated in focal \(20\%\)-active modules (NonnegPartsWeak and Shared+Private), increasing the quantile threshold to \(q = 0.8\) raises support recovery to \(F_1 = 0.840\) while preserving \(99.1\%\) of peak subspace accuracy (\(0.673\) vs. \(0.679\)).

Comparing the unsupervised anatomical baselines against cognitive-aligned SiMR models in Table 3.3 and Figure 3.5 yields three core clinical and neurobiological insights:

Supervising MRI Factor Discovery with Cognitive Batteries Improves Out-of-Sample MRI Prediction by \(+65.8\%\): Unsupervised PCA on the \(382\) structural MRI features explains \(R^2 = 0.152 \pm 0.004\) of out-of-sample cognitive variance on the linear probe and collapses to \(R^2 = 0.044\) on the single-axis Random Forest probe because its leading component reflects global head and brain size rather than focal neurodegeneration. Aligning the MRI projections against the 11-scale cognitive battery during training raises out-of-sample MRI-only CogPC1 prediction to \(R^2 = 0.252 \pm 0.008\) (LEND), \(0.231 \pm 0.015\) (Flow-SiMR-V, with Random Forest axis \(R^2 = 0.197\), a \(4.5\times\) improvement over PCA), and \(0.241\) for linear SiMLR solvers in the \(1,214\)-configuration sweep, while raising mean prediction across all eleven individual cognitive scales by \(+32.1\%\) (\(R^2 = 0.107\) vs. \(0.081\) for PCA; peaking on ADAS13 \(R^2 = 0.195\), ADAS11 \(0.165\), and MMSE \(0.141\)).
Quantile-Sparsified Non-Negative SiMR (\(q = 0.85\)) Isolates Three Classical Braak Neurofibrillary Networks: As shown in Figure 3.5, dense PCA assigns nearly uniform negative weights (\(\approx -0.15\)) across all \(62\) DKT cortical thickness parcels on Component 1 (\(0\%\) sparsity), mixing temporoparietal association areas with primary motor and visual cortices. In contrast, setting sparseness = 0.85 with non-negative nsa_flow (\(w = 0.50\)) restricts each latent axis to exactly \(9/62\) active DKT regions (\(85.5\%\)–\(95.2\%\) sparsity, Gram defect \(D = 8.2 \times 10^{-5}\)) while achieving higher out-of-sample cognitive accuracy (\(R^2 = 0.192\)) than dense PCA (\(0.190\)):

Component 1 (\(\mathbf{v}_1\), Temporoparietal Association Network — Braak Stages IV–V): Concentrates weight in left_middle_temporal (\(+0.670\)), left_supramarginal (\(+0.454\)), right_middle_temporal (\(+0.341\)), right_pars_opercularis (\(+0.319\)), and left_superior_frontal (\(+0.209\)). Thinning across these heteromodal temporoparietal and inferior frontal hubs marks the clinical transition from isolated amnestic impairment to language, semantic, and praxis decline (Braak and Braak 1991; Dickerson et al. 2009; Buckner et al. 2005).
Component 2 (\(\mathbf{v}_2\), Medial Temporal Amnestic Core — Braak Stages I–III): Isolates bilateral entorhinal cortex (left_entorhinal \(+0.680\), right_entorhinal \(+0.226\)) and precuneal/cuneal posterior hubs (right_cuneus \(+0.698\)), coupled with subcortical hippocampal volume loss in View 0 (right_hippocampus \(+0.369\)). This circuit directly reflects early transentorhinal tau neurofibrillary pathology responsible for episodic memory encoding failure on RAVLT and ADASQ4 (Braak and Braak 1991; Jack et al. 2018; Rey 1964).
Component 3 (\(\mathbf{v}_3\), Frontocingulate Salience Network): Targets left_rostral_middle_frontal (\(+0.631\)), right_caudal_anterior_cingulate (\(+0.478\)), and bilateral insular cortex (left_insula \(+0.434\), right_insula \(+0.429\)). Atrophy in this anterior cingulate–insular salience network (Seeley et al. 2009; Menon and Uddin 2010) governs executive set-shifting deficits (TRABSCOR (Reitan 1958)) and everyday functional decline (FAQ (Pfeffer et al. 1982)).

Spared Primary Sensorimotor Cortex Acts as an Internal Negative Control: Across all three components, primary motor cortex (right_precentral \(+0.0016\), left_precentral \(\le 10^{-5}\)) and primary somatosensory cortex (left_postcentral \(\le 10^{-5}\), right_postcentral \(\le 10^{-5}\)) receive effectively zero weight (Figure 3.5 B). Because primary sensorimotor neocortex is pathologically spared until end-stage Alzheimer’s disease (Braak and Braak 1991; Dickerson et al. 2009), its automatic exclusion confirms that non-negative nsa_flow sparsity captures disease-specific vulnerability rather than arbitrary geometric parcellations.

In MultiOmics (TCGA-BRCA, \(N = 822\)), Flow-SiMR-V, LEND, and NEDPP achieve \(92.7\% \pm 0.7\%\) out-of-sample Estrogen Receptor classification accuracy (vs. \(91.5\%\) for PCA), while the sparse non-negative dictionaries \(\mathbf{V}_m\) isolate the canonical luminal breast cancer signaling cascade across all three molecular layers (detailed in Appendix A): estrogen receptor alpha (ER-alpha) and phosphorylated ER-alpha_pS118 in RPPA proteomics, master luminal transcription factors GATA3, PGR, and ESR1 in mRNA transcriptomics (Perou et al. 2000; Parker et al. 2009), and focal chromosomal amplifications at 17q23 and 8p11-p12 in somatic copy-number variation (The Cancer Genome Atlas Network 2012; Curtis et al. 2012). In TCGA-KIRC (\(N = 467\)), adding non-linear decoding in LEND improves pathologic stage classification on the consensus embedding \(\mathbf{U}\) to \(71.4\% \pm 0.4\%\) (vs. \(67.1\%\) for PCA), capturing non-linear metabolic and hypoxia-inducible interactions across transcriptomic and proteomic layers (The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network 2013). title: 4  Discussion and Practical Guidelines
text:
4.1 Synthesizing Clinical Neurobiology and Statistical Representation Learning
The empirical results across ADNI-MCI, TCGA-BRCA, TCGA-KIRC, and the synthetic ground-truth benchmarks demonstrate that predictive accuracy and mechanistic localization do not need to be traded against one another when multi-view integration is organized around an explicit linear entrypoint (\(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\)). For the clinical neuroscientist or neuropsychologist, the primary value of SiMR lies in how cross-modal supervision shapes the learned anatomical basis. When structural MRI is decomposed in isolation via PCA, the dominant axis reflects diffuse global cortical thickness and intracranial scaling across all \(62\) DKT parcels (\(0\%\) sparsity), explaining only \(R^2 = 0.152\) of composite cognitive severity (CogPC1) and collapsing to \(R^2 = 0.044\) under single-axis decision tree splits. By coupling structural MRI views to an 11-scale cognitive battery during training (Protocol B) and applying non-negative approximate Stiefel regularization (nsa_flow, \(w = 0.50, q = 0.85\)), the learned projection matrices isolate three non-redundant, \(88\%\)-sparse anatomical systems that mirror classical Braak neurofibrillary staging (Braak and Braak 1991; Dickerson et al. 2009; Jack et al. 2018): the lateral temporoparietal association circuit (Braak IV–V), the entorhinal–hippocampal amnestic core (Braak I–III), and the fronto-insular-cingulate salience network (Seeley et al. 2009; Menon and Uddin 2010), while automatically zeroing out pathologically spared primary motor and somatosensory cortex.
For the machine learning researcher, our four-probe evaluation resolves why post-hoc rotation or unmixing steps (ICA (Hyvärinen and Oja 2000), orthogonal Procrustes rotations (Schönemann 1966), or dense SVD factors) often appear competitive under ridge regression yet fail when individual coordinates are inspected or thresholded. Because \(\operatorname{span}(\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m \mathbf{M}) = \operatorname{span}(\mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m)\) for any invertible \(\mathbf{M} \in \mathrm{GL}(k)\), linear subspace probes measure only aggregate subspace capacity. Pairing linear subspace probes with coordinate-aligned Random Forest probes (RF(XV)) and ground-truth support recovery (\(F_1\)) exposes diagonal coordinate mixing directly: across all twelve benchmarks, nsa_flow-regularized architectures cut the axis-sensitivity drop in half (\(\Delta = -0.022\) vs. \(-0.044\) for PCA) while recovering up to \(84.7\%\) of true pathway supports.

section: 4.3 Limitations and Negative Findings
text:
4.3 Limitations and Negative Findings
Rigorous experimental reporting requires highlighting the regimes where SiMR architectures underperform, incur computational trade-offs, or require careful preprocessing:

No Universal Advantage Over PCA on Unaligned Single-View Unsupervised Tasks: When a single homogeneous data matrix is analyzed without cross-modal supervision or when views share identical signal-to-noise ratios and dense Gaussian loadings, standard PCA remains optimal for variance explanation in \(\mathcal{O}(\min(N p^2, p N^2))\) time (\(0.004\text{ s}\)). Similarly, on low-dimensional clinical tables such as Heart (\(p = [7, 6]\)), NSAFlow-PCA (\(0.848\)) slightly exceeds multi-view SiMLR (\(0.831\)) because cross-view graph regularization adds variance when \(p_m\) is very small.
Global Cortical Thickness Confounding Without Quantile Thresholding (\(q = \text{None}\)): On ADNI-MCI, running non-negative SiMLR with sparseness = None leaves Component 1 \(85.5\%\) dense (\(55/62\) active DKT regions) because cortical thickness parcels share a positive global correlation floor across the brain. Removing this global floor requires either setting the quantile threshold to \(q \in [0.50, 0.85]\) (which strips the diffuse background floor while raising CogPC1 \(R^2\) from \(0.189\) to \(0.192\)–\(0.209\)) or applying in-fold subject row-mean centering (which yields uniform \(68\%\)–\(76\%\) sparsity across all components but reduces CogPC1 \(R^2\) from \(0.189\) to \(0.153\) by discarding global atrophy severity, as shown in Appendix B).
Stiffness and Accuracy Degradation at Extreme Orthogonality Weights (\(w \ge 0.80\)): Pushing the nsa_flow trade-off weight toward strict Stiefel projection (\(w = 0.95\)) increases wall-clock optimization time by \(2.5\times\)–\(3.8\times\) due to boundary stiffness on the non-negative orthant and reduces ADNI-MCI CogPC1 \(R^2\) from \(0.159\) (\(w = 0.50\)) to \(0.132\) (\(w = 0.95\)). Conversely, setting \(w \le 0.10\) triggers severe rank collapse (\(\text{EffRank} = 2.02\) of \(k = 3\), Gram defect \(D = 0.244\)). The balanced default \(w = 0.50\) avoids both failure modes across all tested cohorts.
Hyperparameter Sensitivity of Deep Multi-View Models on Small Sample Sizes: When sample sizes are moderate (\(N \le 400\) in NonnegParts and Heart), deep autoencoder variants (NED, NEDPP) exhibit higher fold-to-fold variance and lower feature support recovery (\(F_1 = 0.587\)–\(0.642\)) than quasi-Newton linear solvers (SiMLR-LBFGSB, \(F_1 = 0.861\)–\(0.991\)).

4.4 Conclusion
By enforcing an explicit, sparse, non-negative, and approximately orthogonal linear projection at the input boundary of every modality, the SiMR framework bridges classical multivariate biostatistics and modern multi-modal representation learning. Clinicians and domain scientists gain immediately auditable neuroanatomical and molecular networks with exact patient-level risk attributions, while machine learning practitioners gain a flexible family of linear, non-linear decoder, and normalizing-flow alignment modules that preserve both subspace capacity and single-axis disentanglement.

text:
C.1 Model Formulation
Flow-SiMR-V prepends a linear entrypoint projection matrix \(\mathbf{V}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{p_m \times k}\) to each view’s volume-preserving Normalizing Flow (Dinh et al. 2017; Rezende and Mohamed 2015; Kingma and Dhariwal 2018; Papamakarios et al. 2021; Kobyzev et al. 2020). This architecture provides a linear bottleneck at the input boundary while retaining bijective density mapping, conditional cross-view inference, and latent trajectory interpolation on the \(k\)-dimensional subspace. The normalizing flows are implemented in PyTorch (Paszke et al. 2019), adapting coupling structures from the Latent-Aligned Multiview Normalizing Flows (LAMNrFlows) framework (ntustison/LAMNrFlows).

title: Appendix C — Normalizing Flow SiMR with Linear Encoder Bottleneck (Flow-SiMR-V)
text:
C.1.1 Mathematical Formulation
For each input modality \(\mathbf{X}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p_m}\) (\(m = 1, \dots, M\)):

Linear entrypoint bottleneck: \[
\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m, \qquad \mathbf{V}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{p_m \times k},
\] where \(\mathbf{V}_m\) is regularized via nsa_flow (\(w \in (0, 1)\), default \(w = 0.5\)) or polar retraction (Higham 2008; Absil et al. 2008).
Low-dimensional bijective normalizing flow: \[
\mathbf{Z}_m = f_{\text{flow}, m}(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}}),
\] where \(f_{\text{flow}, m}: \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^k\) is a composition of RealNVP affine coupling layers (Dinh et al. 2017) with exact inverse \(f_{\text{flow}, m}^{-1}\) and tractable log-determinant \(\log |\det J_{f_{\text{flow}, m}}(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}})|\).
Consensus mixing and inverse reconstruction: \[
\mathbf{U}_m = \operatorname{Consensus}\big(\{\mathbf{Z}_j\}_{j \in \mathcal{N}(m)}\big), \qquad \hat{\mathbf{X}}_m = f_{\text{flow}, m}^{-1}(\mathbf{U}_m) \mathbf{V}_m^\top.
\]

section: C.2 Rectangular OLEE Prior Collapse and Detached-Prior Optimization
text:
C.2 Rectangular OLEE Prior Collapse and Detached-Prior Optimization
A structural distinction separates square ambient-space normalizing flows (Flow-SiMR, where \(f_{\text{flow},m}: \mathbb{R}^{p_m} \to \mathbb{R}^{p_m}\)) from rectangular OLEE-bottlenecked flows (Flow-SiMR-V, where \(\mathbf{V}_m \in \mathbb{R}^{p_m \times k}\) with \(k \ll p_m\) precedes \(f_{\text{flow},m}: \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}^k\)).

C.2.1 Why End-to-End Gaussian Prior Gradients Collapse \(\mathbf{V}_m\)
In standard normalizing flows, maximum likelihood training minimizes the negative log-likelihood under a standard isotropic Gaussian prior \(p(\mathbf{z}) = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I}_k)\): \[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{NLL}}(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}}; f_{\text{flow},m}) = \frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^n \|f_{\text{flow},m}(\mathbf{z}_{m,\text{lin},i})\|_2^2 - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \log \left|\det \frac{\partial f_{\text{flow},m}}{\partial \mathbf{z}_{m,\text{lin}}}(\mathbf{z}_{m,\text{lin},i})\right|.
\] When the rectangular projection \(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}} = \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m\) (\(k \ll p_m\)) precedes the flow, the change-of-variables determinant \(\log |\det J_{f_{\text{flow},m}}|\) accounts only for volume changes inside the \(k\)-dimensional subspace and contains no log-determinant term for the rectangular projection \(\mathbf{V}_m\). If \(\nabla_{\mathbf{V}_m} \mathcal{L}_{\text{NLL}}\) is backpropagated into \(\mathbf{V}_m\), the quadratic penalty \(\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{Z}_m\|_2^2 = \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{V}_m^\top \mathbf{X}_m^\top \mathbf{X}_m \mathbf{V}_m) + \mathcal{O}(\|f_{\text{flow},m} - \mathrm{id}\|)\) is minimized by rotating \(\mathbf{V}_m\) onto the trailing eigenvectors of \(\mathbf{X}_m^\top \mathbf{X}_m\) with the smallest eigenvalues \(\lambda_{p_m-k+1}, \dots, \lambda_{p_m}\).


C.2.2 Detached-Prior Subspace-Decoupled Optimization
To prevent rectangular prior collapse, Flow-SiMR-V detaches \(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}}\) at the input to the Gaussian prior penalty:

OLEE basis update (\(\mathbf{V}_m\)): Updated exclusively by the cross-view alignment energy \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}\) and within-view relative reconstruction loss \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}}\), while detaching \(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}}\) in the prior term (\(\operatorname{sg}(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}}) = \mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}}.\text{detach}()\)).
Bijective flow update (\(f_{\text{flow},m}\)): Trained via \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{NLL}}(f_{\text{flow},m}(\operatorname{sg}(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}}))) + \mathcal{L}_{\text{align}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{recon}}\), initialized with zero scale and translation weights (\(s_\ell = 0, t_\ell = 0\)) at epoch \(0\) so \(f_{\text{flow},m}^{(0)}(\mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}}) = \mathbf{Z}_{m,\text{lin}}\).

In the ADNI-MCI 1,214-configuration sweep (\(N = 1,084\), \(k = 3\), Protocol B), Flow-SiMR-V with detached-prior optimization reaches an out-of-sample CogPC1 \(R^2\) of \(0.2341\) (Mean11_RidgeCV \(= 0.1054\), and \(0.1930 \pm 0.0048\) across the 3-seed benchmark), ranking third overall across all 12 benchmark datasets.

C.3.1 Conditional Clinical Imputation (True vs. Imputed Serums)
Because Flow-SiMR-V preserves invertibility on the \(k\)-dimensional bottleneck space, it supports conditional cross-view inference via the Gaussian Schur complement in latent space. In Figure C.1, we train Flow-SiMR-V on the Diabetes dataset under a 70/30 split, withhold the blood serum view on test patients, and impute serum triglycerides (s5) from vitals alone.








Figure C.1: Invertible normalizing flows enable accurate conditional cross-view imputation from vitals to blood serum via latent Gaussian conditioning. Scatter plot compares True vs. Imputed Serum triglyceride levels (s5) for \(N_{\text{test}} = 133\) held-out test patients in the Diabetes dataset (70/30 train/test split, \(k = 2\)). The horizontal axis plots true standardized serum levels; the vertical axis plots imputed levels decoded through the Flow-SiMR-V Schur complement solver. Red dashed line indicates the identity reference (\(y = x\)). Preserving latent invertibility allows unobserved biological views to be recovered from observed physical measurements.







C.3.2 Patient-Level Linear Attribution
Prepending the linear encoder matrix \(\mathbf{V}_m\) ensures that the normalizing flow coupling layers do not obscure feature importance at the input boundary. Figure C.2 displays the local feature contributions \(\mathbf{x}_{m,i} \odot \mathbf{v}_{m,l}\) for a patient in the Heart Disease cohort.








Figure C.2: Normalizing flow architectures retain direct input-boundary feature attribution by restricting non-linearity to downstream latent transforms. Horizontal bar chart shows elementwise linear attributions \(\mathbf{x}_{m,i} \odot \mathbf{v}_{m,l}\) for Patient #1 on View 1 of the Heart Disease cohort (\(N = 303\), features age, sex, cp, trestbps). The horizontal axis plots linear contribution values; the vertical axis lists features. Red bars denote positive risk contributions (cp chest pain); blue bars denote negative contributions. Prepending the linear dictionary \(\mathbf{V}_m\) guarantees that normalizing flow coupling layers do not obscure input-boundary transparency.







C.3.3 Latent Trajectory Interpolation
Tracing a straight-line interpolation in the shared latent space between a low-risk and high-risk patient and inverting it through \(f_{\text{flow},m}^{-1}\) and \(\mathbf{V}_m^\top\) defines a smooth trajectory in feature space (Figure C.3).

Decoded biomarker trajectories along a straight-line latent interpolation path between Patient #0 (low-risk, \(\alpha = 0.0\)) and Patient #10 (high-risk, \(\alpha = 1.0\)) on the Diabetes cohort (\(k = 2\)). The horizontal axis plots the latent trajectory coordinate \(\alpha \in [0, 1]\); the vertical axis plots standardized feature levels. text:
D.2 Non-Parametric Benchmark Engine and Optimization Stack
All statistical hypothesis tests, ranking matrices, and permutation null distributions are computed by src/pysimlr/benchmarks/deep_ranking.py:

Non-parametric Friedman omnibus test (Friedman 1937) and Iman–Davenport \(F\)-distribution extension (Demšar 2006; Iman and Davenport 1980).
Two-tailed Nemenyi Critical Difference (\(CD = 3.468\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\) for \(k = 9, B = 12\)) (Nemenyi 1963; Demšar 2006).
Pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests (Wilcoxon 1945) with Holm–Bonferroni step-down adjustments (Holm 1979).
Quasi-Newton (L-BFGS, L-BFGS-B (Byrd et al. 1995; Nocedal and Wright 2006)) and adaptive first-order (Adam, AdamW (Kingma and Ba 2015; Loshchilov and Hutter 2019)) solvers implemented on top of PyTorch (Paszke et al. 2019), NumPy (Harris et al. 2020), SciPy (Virtanen et al. 2020), and Scikit-Learn (Pedregosa et al. 2011).
Benchmark cohorts span clinical cardiology (Heart (Detrano et al. 1989)), metabolic progression (Diabetes (Efron et al. 2004)), handwritten pattern descriptors (mfeat (Breukelen et al. 1998)), transcriptomic/multi-omic cancer benchmarks (Golub et al. 1999; The Cancer Genome Atlas Network 2012; The Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network 2013; Wang et al. 2014; Tenenhaus and Tenenhaus 2011; Tenenhaus et al. 2014; Zhao et al. 2017; Abdi et al. 2013), and Alzheimer’s neuroimaging (ADNI-MCI (Mueller et al. 2005; Jack et al. 2008; Weiner et al. 2017)).

The test suite tests/test_deep_ranking_stats.py verifies the statistical calculations:
pytest tests/test_deep_ranking_stats.py -v

D.3.1 Block-Level Sign-Flip Permutation Floor
In paired comparisons across \(B = 12\) independent dataset blocks (where each block cell is the mean across \(N_{\text{seeds}} = 3\) replicates (Demšar 2006)), the exact distribution-free sign-flip null distribution across the \(B = 12\) blocks consists of \(2^B = 4,096\) sign assignments:
\[
p_{\text{perm}} = \frac{1}{2^B} \sum_{\mathbf{s} \in \{-1, +1\}^B} \mathbb{I}\left(\left|\frac{1}{B} \sum_{i=1}^B s_i \Delta_i\right| \ge |\bar{\Delta}|\right), \qquad p_{\min, B=12} = \frac{2}{2^{12}} = \frac{2}{4096} \approx 0.000488
\]
